Q: Concurrent cache using SoftReferences behaves unpredictably under memory pressure, how to fix? A:
  • Sometimes objects disappear from the cache unexpectedly, even when memory usage is low.

This is what the API docs say about when soft references are cleared:

All soft references to softly-reachable objects are guaranteed to have been cleared before the virtual machine throws an OutOfMemoryError. Otherwise no constraints are placed upon the time at which a soft reference will be cleared or the order in which a set of such references to different objects will be cleared. Virtual machine implementations are, however, encouraged to bias against clearing recently-created or recently-used soft references.

(Emphasis added.)

It is therefore unclear what basis you have for expectations about when soft references to softly reachable objects in your cache will be cleared. Certainly the docs do not require memory pressure for clearance of soft references to softly reachable objects, and neither does the Oracle / OpenJDK implementation.

  • Occasionally, cleanup() causes high CPU usage under heavy load.

It should not be surprising that iterating through a large map is expensive. Especially so a concurrent map with contended access, and even more so if many modifications are made along the way.

Iterating the whole map is not at all what you should be doing here. If you register your SoftReferences with a reference queue then you can discover exactly which ones to remove from the cache by obtaining them from that queue. And if you subclass SoftReference then you can endow yours with references to the corresponding cache keys, so that you know which entries to remove without searching at all.

You could optionally avoid having an explicit cleanup() method at all by establishing a thread devoted to retrieving references to the queue as they become available and removing them immediately.

  • I’m not sure this is thread-safe when cleanup() runs concurrently with get() and put().

ConcurrentHashMap is thread safe in the sense that no data races arise from multiple threads performing operations on the same instance concurrently. Individual actions by one thread have their documented behavior regardless of actions by other threads. However, sequences of actions on a ConcurrentHashMap by one thread can suffer from interference from intervening actions by other threads unless some additional mechanism is employed to prevent it. This is not different from a Hashtable or a synchronized Map provided by Collections.synchronizedMap(). In your case, nothing in the specs for ConcurrentHashMap guarantees that the state of the map observed by your entry.getValue().get() is the same state affected by the subsequent it.remove(). Suppose, then, that a thread retrieves a SoftReference from the cache, observes it to have been cleared, and therefore constructs and caches a new a new one. It is possible that in the meantime, a thread running cleanup() also notices the cleared reference and therefore moves to drop it from the cache, but instead ends up removing the newly cached one. A similar sequence of events could result in distinct objects for the same key being live at the same time.

These are not necessarily failure cases for you per se, so maybe you don't want to account them thread safety issues, but they could certainly make your cache less effective.

  • Are there any concurrency issues with this implementation, especially with hundreds of threads?

See above. But also, hundreds of concurrently running platform threads could be its own concurrency issue. Context switching is expensive.

  • How do SoftReferences interact with GC under different memory pressures? Why might cached objects disappear unexpectedly?

Under sufficient memory pressure, SoftReferences to softly-reachable objects may be cleared sooner than they otherwise would be. Lack of memory pressure is not a good reason to think that soft references will go uncleared indefinitely.

Q: matplotlib axes3d how to use all window space plotting A:

There is a related post on matplotlib's discourse: How to turn off all clipping?.

As the first answerer to that thread wrote, basically "some clipping is [always] desired", meaning that all objects drawn by matplotlib have some clipping enabled by default, which makes sense.

Both answers then suggest to call set_clip_on(False) on all child objects of a figure, but that seems a bit of an overshoot.

I have almost no experience with matplotlib, but after seeing that thread and checking the documentation about plot_wireframe() and the related sources, that function doesn't just "Plot a 3D wireframe" as the docs suggest: it also returns a Line3DCollection object, with its clipping property active, as expected.

Since that is what you're probably interested in, a quick test showed that it may be enough to simply call set_clip_on() on that object.

The following change in the plot_wire() function should then suffice:

    def plot_wire(self):
        # Data
        self.X, self.Y, self.Z = axes3d.get_test_data(0.03)

        wireframe = self._ax.plot_wireframe(
            self.X, self.Y, self.Z, rstride=10, cstride=10, cmap="viridis")
        wireframe.set_clip_on(False)

        self.canvas.draw()

Q: How to disable new 'modal window' in VSCode A:

Use the shortcut:

Press Ctrl plus Shift plus P >Type Preferences Open Settings JSON.

This always opens settings in a normal editor tab.

VS Code does not offer a switch to turn this UI off. The JSON editor is the only clean workaround today.

Q: Getting all the rows from the table in addition with min and max value A:

The answer to your question is yes it is possible but its probably not the best way to do it (I believe this solution will place more work on your DB queries - which if they're not optimised could be quite expensive (in terms of time/CPU)).

$this->db->select('price,title,date,(SELECT MAX(price) FROM '.$this->price.') as MinPrice,(SELECT MIN(price) FROM '.$this->price.') as MaxPrice);
